source.title: GROM: Gradient-Free Rapid One-Shot Machine Unlearning
source.authors: Pawel Batorski; P. Spurek; Paul Swoboda

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some table formatting is flattened, but the relevant Table 6 values can be assigned to their rows and metrics.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether quantization restores forgotten knowledge and finds a sharp difference between SimNPO and GROM, qualifying the claim that quantization generally recovers hidden knowledge.
record.gate_note: The relevant original results are the full-precision and 4-bit MUSE measurements in Table 6. The paper also discusses quantization results from Zhang et al. (2025), but those cited results are not recorded as study results. Other benchmark results concern GROM's forgetting and utility trade-offs, not recovery by the attacks in the claim.
record.test_reason: The study applies 4-bit quantization (reproducing Zhang et al. 2025) to SimNPO- and GROM-unlearned MUSE models. It reports forget-set memorization before and after (Table 6), so its own results bear on D (quantization recovery), on A (whether simple attacks recover forgotten content), and on F (GROM claimed robust). Quantization recovers content for SimNPO but not for GROM, which restricts where D holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that 4-bit quantization restores much of what SimNPO appeared to forget, while GROM stays as forgetful as Retrain. They take this as evidence that the closed-form edit removes rather than hides content. Their added claim that retain utility drops at 4-bit for every method is contradicted by their own Table 6 for SimNPO (News 39.65→47.4, Books 48.27→52.4).
record.recipe_differences: GROM uses a closed-form weight edit rather than iterative unlearning; the quantization comparison applies 4-bit quantization to GROM and SimNPO on MUSE News and MUSE Books.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by unlearning method and MUSE corpus: SimNPO shows large VerbMem Df recovery under quantization, while GROM does not; KnowMem Df changes are smaller than VerbMem Df changes.
record.problems: The quantization evidence is limited to 4-bit and two MUSE corpora. Table 6 reports no uncertainty estimates. The study reports that retain utility drops at 4-bit for every method, including Original and Retrain, so quantization also affects retained performance.

untested.parts: Only the 4-bit quantization attack is tested, on MUSE memorization metrics. Not tested: WMDP accuracy recovery, relearning, prompting or internal-edit attacks.
No direction ablation or analysis of blocking versus deletion beyond quantization.
Only 4-bit precision; no 8-bit or other widths. Only SimNPO and GROM; no other gradient methods. Only MUSE; no TOFU or WMDP.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context attacks.
GROM's robustness is tested only against quantization. Fine-tuning, internal edits and prompting attacks are not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The record misassigned the flattened Table 6 blocks; Final Score arithmetic confirms the correct mapping. Rows r3/r4/r7/r8/r11/r12/r15/r16 are News KnowMem Dr (utility), not KnowMem Df. Rows r19–r32 KnowMem values are MUSE News KnowMem Df, not Books. The real Books KnowMem Df values are unrecorded. The record's version codes V1/V4/V6 map to A/D/F. Evidence uses a single run with no uncertainty. Only 4-bit and SimNPO are compared with GROM. The paper is a method preprint whose quantization test is a secondary robustness check.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests recovery by 4-bit quantization on MUSE using memorization measures, not targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance across other methods or attack types.
Fine-tuning or relearning attacks are not tested.
Ablating an activation direction and testing whether unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge are not tested.
The quantization test is 4-bit on two MUSE corpora and compares SimNPO with GROM; other bit widths, methods, and settings are not tested.
Prompt rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, and in-context information are not tested as recovery attacks.
GROM's resistance is tested against quantization only, not fine-tuning, internal edits, or prompting attacks.
